en: Her black hair like sedge
She bound tightly atop her head.
If an enemy came out to shoot,
They drove the enemy back together.
Your dear mother Kanykei—
Which of her deeds shall we tell?
She made her mourning head a banner,
Made a woman's self a hero.
Heroically built, an extraordinary warrior,
When I stoop, I have no saddle,
An arrow loosed in many battles.
That precious mother of yours, Kanykei,
Was an accomplished woman,
The daughter of Temir Khan.
The youngest of twelve daughters,
A servant beloved of God,
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims,
The most graceful in tasseled ornaments,
The finest among women,
The best of all called wives,
The sovereign among women.
Can an ordinary woman be like this?
Can one who calls her merely a woman prosper?
Whoever calls her merely a woman,
Will he ever prosper in any year?
By the time she left Bukhara,
She had gathered her courage,
Mounted a different horse,
And donned a hero's clothing.
Wrathful and forbidding,
As though she would slaughter Bukhara,
She girded on an iron belt,
Turned outward, revealing no secrets.
‘On my right are Russians;
Before me are Franks.
Many enemies wait to contend with me.
If anyone attacks my only son,
Let me die if my appointed death has come;
If I have a means, let me try it.
For the poor child gained through mortal suffering,
Let me serve as a protector.
Between Talas and Bukhara
Lies a considerable road,
And many enemies to contend with.’
Preparing her equipment,
All her weapons
She fastened on in readiness.
Your extraordinary mother Kanykei
Led Chachykei along.
The cherished bride Chachykei,
In changing hues of red and many colors,
She dressed in crimson cloth,
The hem of the crimson cloth
She let trail slantwise upon the ground.
Appearing mottled green,
She dressed her in pure silk,
And the hem of that silk
She spread to touch the ground.
Upon your Chachy's head,
She placed the bridal headdress.
Along the headdress's rim,
Red gold could be seen.
Whoever caught sight of her
Had his heart greatly diverted.
Down her back, the braid coverings
Fell in six separate strands.
The cherished Chachykei
She dressed in many colors.
If you would see splendor, see it here:
When they moved away from Bukhara,
She gave her Taitoru to ride.
Setting their faces toward Talas,
Semetey, the son of Manas,
Rode Buurul, making him toss,
Making him struggle like a bereaved wife.
Akolpok and Akkelte
Could be seen upon him.
Manas's son was a hero,
A lion who had studied his lessons,
His father, magnanimous Manas—
He was a hero born surpassing him.
A leopard with a guardian spirit,
My saint who could not be shaken—
The company traveled toward Talas,
Going far without tiring,
Wearing horses down, covering ground,
Unleashing hounds and flying birds.
The horse he rode beneath him—
His father Manas, carried away in fury,
Had left that peerless steed behind.
What he held in his hand,
Encountered through the unseen,
Found in the open wilderness,
A kite had hatched and reared into a falcon.
By God's decree, the child
Had met it in the empty steppe:
It was Semetey's falcon.
Your heroic lord, the son of Manas,
Saying, ‘Spring has come,
The land is full of greenery,
The migrating swans, geese and ducks
Have made twelve years.
I am setting out upon my journey,’
The son of Manas took no heed.
If an enemy came out firing,
Or a shouting giant appeared,
He did not rate them at his heel.
Courage and insolent pride
To the orphan son of Manas,
God Most High, the Almighty,
Had given without measure.
Your orphan, the son of Manas,
Unleashing hounds and flying birds,
Went on without a care.
The white falcon in his hand,
The treasury his mother Kanykei had hidden,
Half silk and half gold,
Had golden jesses on its feet.
It wrought slaughter among swans,
And had enemies such as cranes.
Its talons were steel, its jess fastener copper;
Nothing it struck escaped alive.
It measured two kez around.
It did not stoop with folded wings;
It let no goose rise from the lake.
It did not stoop with spread tail;
It let no swan rise from the lake.
It tired the arm that held it;
Released, it satisfied the heart.
The white falcon in his hand—
‘It will know my worth,
And fly about keeping me in sight,’ he thought.
He cast it out toward the open country,
And thrust it away to the far side.
The white falcon left his hand,
Rose and set its course,
As though it had lost sight of him.
Circling, gliding,
Your oceanlike hero's white falcon
Flew away, leaning back in the air.
Manas's heroic orphan son,
On the near side of Bukhara,
Three days' journey this side of it,
Where the rough hillocks
Came to an end at a spur,
At a jutting stand of thick chiy grass,
The land was full of greenery.
Along that stretch of land,
Grazing like sheep in their thousands,
Bustards filled the place, waddling about.
Now the spectacle was complete.
At those walking bustards,
Manas Khan's Kumaiyk
Arrived and sent them scattering.
With a thunder that hid the ground,
The bustards took flight.
The white falcon reached and struck them,
Striking each one it overtook,
While Kumaiyk went biting them.
Your orphan, the son of Manas,
Pounded Taibuurul onward,
Shouting, ‘Manas! Manas!’
Raising ‘Manas!’ as his battle cry,
Semetey went shouting his cry.
Letting no bustards or other birds escape,
The white falcon pursued them,
Striking this way and that.
The slaughtered bustards and other birds
Kumaiyk went gathering up.
Your orphan, the son of Manas,
Was filled with joy.
Kanykei in her advancing years,
Chiyyrdy in her old age,
Sary Khan with his bowl-like eyes,
The behavior of Khan Sary -
All four shared in the spectacle.
On the plain smooth as a blade,
Who had seen such a spectacle!
Their servant lads who tended the camels
Also came to a halt.
Marveling at the entertainment,
They stood watching in amazement:
‘Whom God has truly created—
It is true that he is His servant.
Of dear lord Manas,
It is true that he is the son!
It is true that his father Manas
Brought the world under his rule.
Allah Most High, making a living soul,
This orphan child—
It is true that He created him!’
Seeing the falcon, Kanykei said:
‘Compared with his khan father's falcon,
This is a keener, more skillful hunter,
A joy and delight when released.
God has relieved my grief;
The child has taken after his father.
He has settled in his place.
This orphan of mine standing here
Has become like my mighty destroyer.
Now I may die without regret;
Not the slightest regret remains in me.
Once, Almighty One,
You let a raven devour my falcon.
The child who came from my womb,
You had called another man's son.
You let a crow devour my swan.
When I fled to Bukhara,
The child who came from my womb,
You made him be called the Sarts' son.
That dear bird called the little bustard
Flies twittering for its young.
I bore such toil, poor soul,
For the child left by the warrior.
That dear bird called the wild duck
Wheels in flight in search of food.
How much I have suffered, poor soul,
For you, who came from my womb.
Ah, my plump little mottled gray goshawk hen,
My gray goshawk, my morning star.
When I was a young bride, my foal,
“Late in life I braided my hair,
You whom I bore so late.
Your father Khan Manas's treasury
Upon the poor and the destitute
I spent and lavished.
When I reached thirty-one,
I asked God for you.
My wide world grew narrow;
I was so long delayed, poor soul,
Yearning for a single child.
At Khan Kokotoi's memorial feast,
Before the great gathering,
A company of holy sages came together;
You were born of their prayers.
All the holy sages joined together;
My orphan, whom I cherish,
You were born of their blessing!
From there we traveled onward;
For six days we traveled far without rest.
There lay the broad plain,
Chong-Ak-Chiy of spacious Bukhara,
A journey of six days away.
The white saddle ridge, like a child's saddle—
I, your mother Kanykei,
Used to keep watch there.
My father Temir Khan's court girls,
Thirty young wives and thirty maidens,
Exceedingly beautiful, all skilled in craft.
She herself was fourteen then.
Beyond Ak-Kaiky
Lay Kanykei's Keng-Kolchuk,
The place she went for pleasure,
Setting up swings and playing much;
The place your unfortunate mother stayed,
